comparisons.peer_topic: FPGA and Adaptive SoC Platform Offerings
comparisons.peer_summary: The company offers FPGAs with reconfigurable hardware and integrated cores, and Adaptive SoCs targeting embedded systems with heterogeneous processing systems for real-time control and acceleration. Specific products include Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoCs for RF applications and the Versal portfolio for heterogeneous acceleration in big data and AI.
comparisons.comparison: Both AVGO and AMD describe platforms that enable customers to design customized hardware solutions for specific workloads, including AI. AVGO focuses on providing the underlying IP and technology platforms (including SerDes and processor cores) for customers to build custom ASICs targeting AI and high-performance computing. AMD offers FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs which provide reconfigurable hardware and integrated cores (like DSP and networking) to support customer designs for similar applications, including big data and AI acceleration. While AVGO's model centers on bespoke ASICs built from its IP portfolio, AMD offers adaptable, reconfigurable hardware platforms (FPGAs/Adaptive SoCs) that allow for customization and acceleration without the full commitment of a custom ASIC design.

sentences.text: • Custom Silicon Solutions: We provide advanced technology and intellectual property ("IP") platforms for customers to design and develop application specific integrated circuits ("ASICs") targeting AI and high-performance computing, networking and storage applications. Our custom silicon provides the platform to integrate embedded logic, memory, serializer/deserializer ("SerDes") technology, IP cores and processor cores. ASICs are custom products built to individual customers specifications.
We offer two types of platforms that support our customers' designs and reduce their development efforts: FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs.
This product portfolio is ideally suited to accelerate a broad set of applications in the emerging era of big data and AI.

peer_results.rationale: Intelligent Edge processor suite and process node development are not comparable to AVGO's custom silicon IP and ASIC platform offerings. INTC's disclosures focus on its own edge CPU products and manufacturing process nodes, whereas AVGO provides IP for customer-designed ASICs. No candidate addresses custom silicon design platforms or IP licensing for ASICs.

comparisons.peer_topic: Data Center AI and High-Performance Storage Offerings
comparisons.peer_summary: Demand for AI and big data is driving the need for high-performance storage; SBU addresses this with the 6500 30TB SSD for AI data lakes and sampled the 9550 series in 2024 for AI and high-performance computing workloads.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies address the infrastructure demands of AI and high-performance computing, though through different product types. AVGO provides the custom silicon (ASICs) and IP platforms (including storage-related IP like SerDes) that underpin these systems. Micron complements this infrastructure with high-performance storage solutions (SSDs) specifically designed for AI data lakes and high-performance computing workloads, noting that AI applications require fast data access with low latency. Both identify AI and HPC as key drivers requiring specialized, high-performance hardware components.

peer_results.rationale: NVIDIA's automotive platform and compute server offerings are distinct from AVGO's custom silicon IP business. While both are involved in AI hardware, NVIDIA sells complete GPUs, systems, and automotive platforms, whereas AVGO provides the embedded logic, memory, and SerDes IP for customers to build their own ASICs. No candidate focuses on the provision of IP/platforms for customer-designed custom integrated circuits.

Qualcomm's System-on-Chip architecture and AI Engine descriptions focus on its own integrated processor designs (CPUs, GPUs, NPUs) for devices and automotive, rather than providing IP platforms for customers to design their own custom ASICs. The comparison is of integrated product architectures versus IP/ASIC enablement platforms, which are substantively different business models and product types.
